newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai editorials lash out at Chavalit, demand change.
newsitem.headline: Thai editorials lash out at Chavalit, demand change.

text.p: Thailand's two major English language newspapers on Wednesday blamed political mismanagement and money politics for the economic crisis and demanded reform or a change in government in order to restore confidence.

Front-page commentaries in the Bangkok Post and The Nation newspapers followed the same line in criticising the country's leaders for bringing the once-booming economy to its lowest growth level in a decade and forcing it to seek aid from the International Monetary Fund (IMF)

"Let's not forget how this country wound up in this sorry debacle in the first place," said the Bangkok Post. "Politicians of all shades -- including (Prime Minister) General Chavalit (Yongchaiyudh) -- are to blame. They have allowed this country to surrender its economic sovereignty because of their gross mismanagement over the past several years."

The commentaries said the series of tough austerity measures announced on Tuesday by the government were necessary for economic recovery, but they questioned how much people could trust the government to actually implement the measures.

"Despite the measures announced yesterday, the fact remains that no one believes this government any more," the Bangkok Post said. "What assurances can the government give to the people to show it, too, is prepared to take the pain?"
The Nation newspaper agreed, noting that the package worked out in conjunction with the IMF "contains pills that taste bitter beyond what the Thai public and the financial market have expected".
It called on Prime Minister Chavalit, who has had two finance ministers and two central bank governors in his eight months in office, to step down soon.

"There is little faith in this government's ability to carry out the IMF package effectively and minimise hardships to the people," it said. "There is little Chavalit can do or show that will make anyone think he can do better than he has.
"It would be better to hand the mandate to someone else to undertake the restoration," it said. "Without trust and confidence, society cannot move forward."
The Bankgok Post agreed, demanding an overhaul of the country's economic management and political reform.
"The politicians, in particular those in government and the prime minister himself, have refused long enough to say where they stand. They must reform or bear the consequences.
